content: This definition was updated by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) in 1990, replacing the earlier standard of 1 atmosphere (101.325 kilopascals). The standard state can be defined at any temperature, but it is most commonly specified at 25 degrees Celsius. It is important to understand that the standard state is an arbitrarily chosen reference point and not a natural zero point. For any given material, the standard state serves as the reference condition for thermodynamic properties such as enthalpy, entropy, and Gibbs free energy, as well as for other material standards. For example, the standard enthalpy of formation for an element in its standard state is defined as zero. If molarity is used, this corresponds to 1 mol·dm⁻³, and if molality is used, it corresponds to 1 mol·kg⁻¹, assuming the solution behaves as if it were infinitely dilute. It is possible, and theoretically valid, to define a different unit of concentration for each species in a reaction. However, when reporting or tabulating data, the specific nature of the standard state must be clearly stated. For example, a standard state involving 1 mol/L of one substance combined with a pure substance (mole fraction = 1) is a hypothetical condition that cannot physically exist. Nevertheless, such a non-existent standard state can still provide a consistent framework for tabulated values, as long as it is applied consistently. It is worth noting that the values derived from one standard state will differ from those based on a different standard state. Historically, during the 19th century, the Plimsoll symbol (°) was introduced as a superscript to indicate the non-zero nature of the chosen reference state. However, for typographical reasons, this symbol has often been simplified to a superscript zero (⁰) in later texts, which can be somewhat misleading.
